difficultyRationale: Requires knowing why the Spring team recommends constructor injection beyond style — the fail-fast startup behavior is the part candidates often can't articulate.
prompt: A legacy Spring Boot 2.5 application has `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` (or uses a Framework configuration that explicitly permits resolving some singleton setter/field cycles). Two singleton beans have a dependency cycle. A teammate proposes switching both from field injection to required constructor injection. What changes at startup, and would the same distinction apply by default in Spring Boot 2.6+?
explanation: When circular references are explicitly allowed, Spring can sometimes construct singleton beans first and inject early references through fields/setters, so some such cycles start successfully. Constructor-only cycles cannot complete either constructor and fail at startup. However, since Spring Boot 2.6, circular dependencies are **disabled by default** (`spring.main.allow-circular-references=false`), so it is wrong to claim that field injection would silently succeed by default in modern Boot. Refactor cycles rather than relying on early references.

options.text: There is no behavioral difference; both forms fail at startup identically if a cycle exists, since Spring resolves every `@Autowired` injection point, whether on a field or a constructor parameter, during one unified instantiation phase before the bean is handed back to the container.
options.explanation: In configurations explicitly allowing early singleton references, setter/field cycles may resolve whereas constructor-only cycles cannot. In modern Boot defaults both fail, which is why the version/configuration scope matters.

options.text: In a configuration explicitly allowing early singleton references, a field/setter cycle can sometimes be resolved using a partially constructed bean, while a required-constructor cycle fails because both constructors need the other bean first; Spring Boot 2.6+ disallows circular references by default, so ordinary field cycles fail too unless explicitly reenabled.
options.explanation: Correct. This is a conditional distinction for configurations permitting early references, not an unconditional Spring Boot default. Constructor injection still makes hard cycles impossible to resolve; modern Boot prohibits cycles by default.

options.text: Constructor injection disables Spring's circular dependency detection entirely, so a cycle between two constructor-injected beans goes unnoticed at startup and only surfaces much later as a NullPointerException once the half-wired object is actually used in production.
options.explanation: This is backwards: constructor injection is what makes Spring detect and reject the cycle immediately, rather than letting it through.

options.text: Field injection throws at startup for any cycle between two singleton beans, while constructor injection automatically resolves the same cycle by substituting a lazy proxy for one of the two dependencies, with no extra configuration required.
options.explanation: Required-constructor cycles cannot be resolved by magically generated lazy proxies; allowing field/setter cycles is conditional, and Boot 2.6+ prohibits them by default.
